planting.note: Also excellent as a fall Gulf Coast crop sown 6-8 weeks before first frost; roots size up fast in cool soil.

directions: An improved French Breakfast-type radish bred for a striking two-tone root: bright scarlet shoulders fading cleanly to white at the tip. The elongated roots stay crisp and mild-flavored even as they size up, resisting the pithiness that hits many spring radishes in warm soil. Direct-sow in cool weather and harvest young for the best color contrast and snap; excellent sliced raw for its visual appeal on a relish tray.

planting.note: Well suited to Gulf Coast fall sowing 6-8 weeks before first frost; performs best in cooler soil rather than spring heat.

directions: An All-America Selections-winning open-pollinated radish prized for round roots in a clear bright pink over crisp white flesh. Its flavor is notably gentle and mild rather than sharp, making it a favorite for market growers selling to customers who find standard radishes too peppery. Strong tops make it easy to bunch for market, and the roots resist splitting even when left in the ground a few extra days.

planting.note: A classic fall storage turnip for the Gulf South; sow in late summer for harvest through winter, sweetens after light frost.

directions: A yellow-fleshed heirloom turnip documented since before 1840, grown for smooth globe roots with fine-grained, sweet flesh unlike the sharper white-fleshed types. Best picked around 3 inches across for peak sweetness and tenderness, though roots can size up to 6 inches for winter storage. Sturdy tops also cook well as greens, giving two harvests from one planting.

planting.note: Grows well as a Gulf Coast fall crop; sow in late summer for harvest through the cool season.

directions: A Scottish heirloom bunching beet, grown for over a century, notable for its striking dark magenta-purple leaves as much as its slender, conical red roots. Bred for rapid early growth so it can be harvested young in bunches rather than left to bulk up like a storage beet. The dramatic foliage doubles as an attractive edible green, sauteed like chard, while the roots are sweet and tender when pulled small.

planting.note: Long season root; in mild Gulf Coast winters can also be sown in fall for a spring harvest.

directions: Bred at England's National Vegetable Research Station specifically for strong resistance to parsnip canker, a fungal disease that disfigures roots of many older varieties in humid climates. Roots are shorter and more bulbous than exhibition types, trading some length for reliability and more uniform shape. Its disease tolerance makes it a practical choice in warm, humid growing regions where canker pressure is high.
sources: UK seed trade catalogs (Thompson and Morgan, Marshalls)

planting.note: Long season root; in mild Gulf Coast winters can also be sown in fall for a spring harvest.

directions: The first F1 hybrid parsnip bred in Britain, combining vigor with smooth, blemish-free skin and strong canker resistance. Roots are wide-shouldered and taper to a short body, staying tender and free of a woody core even at large sizes. It has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit and is popular with both home gardeners and show growers for its consistency.
sources: UK seed trade catalogs (Thompson and Morgan, Mr Fothergill's)

planting.note: Suits Gulf Coast fall sowing in loose beds; fast-maturing baby type also works for succession spring plantings.

directions: A Dutch Nantes-type carrot bred with an especially small core, giving straight, uniform roots with fine grain and reliable sweetness. It matures quickly enough to be pulled small as a baby carrot or left slightly longer for full-size roots without losing tenderness. Its short stature and forgiving root shape make it a good fit for heavier or shallower garden soils that stunt longer carrot types.

planting.note: Long-season root best started in mid to late summer for a Gulf Coast fall-through-winter harvest; flavor improves after frost.

directions: Also sold under the name Major Dunne, this Scottish-origin swede was once a commercial variety in the British Isles before falling out of the seed trade and being preserved by seed-saving networks. Roots are more elongated than a typical rutabaga, with smooth golden-tan skin and purple shoulders, standing tall above the soil with vigorous leafy tops. It retains good texture and mild, sweet flavor even when roots are allowed to grow quite large.
